name: brittanychiang.com
object_type: Portfolio — a pure personal portfolio / online resume for an employed senior engineer. It sells nothing, hosts no product funnel, and has no services page. Its only jobs are (a) to be a credible, scannable professional record and (b) to be itself a demonstration of the craft it claims (accessible, pixel-perfect frontend). Secondarily and unintentionally it has become a design template artifact — the single most cloned SE portfolio layout on GitHub — but the current v5 build is not distributed as a template.
format_genre: Document/CV as a scroll-page. A single-page, two-column resume: a fixed/sticky left rail (name, title, tagline, in-page nav, social row) beside a right column that scrolls through About → Experience → Projects → Writing → colophon. No terminal, no 3D, no OS simulation. The layout reads as a well-typeset résumé that happens to live in a browser, which is the defining structural choice the imitators copy.
intent_audience: Personal brand / authority-building, with passive job-seeking as a floor. Evidence for 'not actively job-seeking': there is no 'hire me', no availability statement, no contact form, no email address anywhere on the site, and the About section states a current role in the present tense ('Currently, I'm a Senior Frontend Engineer at Klaviyo'). Evidence it still serves recruiters: a real 2-page PDF résumé is linked ('View Full Résumé'), the Experience section is dated and complete back to 2015, and a full /archive page lists every project by year, employer and stack. The audience is effectively three-layered: recruiters/hiring managers who need the record; peers who read it as a craft demo (a11y-focused engineer proving a11y); and the very large downstream population of developers looking for a layout to copy.
seniority_stage: Senior/staff individual contributor. Currently Senior Frontend Engineer, Accessibility at Klaviyo (2024 — present); previously Lead Engineer → Senior Engineer → Engineer at Upstatement (2018–2024), with co-ops at Apple, Starry and MullenLowe (2015–2017). Roughly a decade of experience, specialised in design systems and web accessibility. 'Good' for this item therefore means: restraint, legibility, evidence of scope/leadership, and zero unforced errors in the craft she is hired for — not novelty. The site is judged on whether its own accessibility and polish back up the résumé's accessibility claim, and it does.
language_i18n: English only. `<html lang="en">`, `og:locale` en_US, no language toggle and no localised routes. The owner is US-based and the entire audience is anglophone, so no i18n is attempted.
owner_role: Brittany Chiang — Senior Frontend Engineer, Accessibility at Klaviyo (Boston, US). Self-described in the hero as 'Frontend Engineer' with the tagline 'I build accessible, pixel-perfect experiences for the web.' Design-system and a11y specialist; formerly Lead Engineer at Upstatement (digital product studio), UI Engineer co-op at Apple (Apple Music web player / MusicKit.js), Software Engineer co-op at Starry, Creative Technologist co-op at MullenLowe. Also author of the paid Newline course 'Build a Spotify Connected App' and of the Halcyon editor theme. Handle `bchiang7` across GitHub/CodePen/Instagram/X.
sections_present: Present: About (a four-paragraph first-person bio with inline links to employers and to a personal Zelda joke), Experience (6 dated roles rendered as a hoverable list with per-role tech tags and inline proof links, plus a 'View Full Résumé' link to /resume.pdf), Projects (4 curated cards with thumbnails, plus 'View Full Project Archive' → /archive, a full sortable-looking table of ~25 projects by Year / Project / Made at / Built with / Link), Writing (4 external articles dated 2019–2026), Contact-by-proxy (a social icon row: GitHub, LinkedIn, CodePen, Instagram, Goodreads), and a colophon crediting Figma, VS Code, Next.js, Tailwind, Vercel and the Inter typeface. Skills section: deliberately ABSENT as a standalone block — skills appear only as tags attached to specific jobs and projects, so every claimed technology is anchored to where it was used. Blog: ABSENT on-site; the Writing section links out to Medium and klaviyo.tech instead of hosting posts. Contact section: ABSENT entirely — no form, no email, no CTA.
nav_pattern: Single-page scroll with two secondary routes (/archive, /resume.pdf). The left rail is `lg:sticky lg:top-0` at 48% width and holds a vertical in-page jump-link nav (About / Experience / Projects) whose labels are uppercase micro-caps with a leading rule that animates on hover and on `:focus-visible`; the nav is wrapped with `aria-label="In-page jump links"`. The right column (`lg:w-[52%]`) is the only thing that scrolls. Critically, the nav is `hidden lg:block` — below the large breakpoint there is no navigation at all, and the page becomes one long linear scroll. Section headings are `lg:sr-only`, i.e. visible as sticky labels on small screens and hidden from sight (but kept for screen readers) on desktop where the rail nav does that job. `scroll-smooth` is set on `<html>` and section anchors carry `scroll-mt` offsets.
visual_style: Restrained dark minimalism — the anti-trend position. It aligns with none of the current portfolio fashions (no bento grid, no neo-brutalism, no glassmorphism, no kinetic typography, no scroll-jacking); its trend alignment is 'editorial minimal', and its influence is such that the two-column dark sticky-rail layout has itself become a recognisable genre. The defining visual devices are all cheap and behavioural rather than decorative: (1) a mouse-tracking spotlight — a `fixed`/`lg:absolute` radial-gradient overlay, `600px circle` of `rgba(29,78,216,0.15)`, following the cursor and disabled below the lg breakpoint; (2) group-hover dimming on the Experience and Projects lists — hovering any row sets the whole list to `opacity-50` and the hovered row back to `!opacity-100`, with a soft card backing (`-inset-x-4 -inset-y-2.5 rounded`) appearing behind it; (3) small pill tech tags in `bg-teal-400/10 text-teal-300`; (4) arrow icons that translate on hover and on focus-visible. Everything is Tailwind utility classes on semantic HTML — no illustration, no 3D, no hero image, no photo of the owner.
color_typography: Fixed dark theme, no light mode and no toggle: `prefers-color-scheme` appears zero times in the shipped CSS. Palette is Tailwind's slate scale plus one accent — `bg-slate-900` (#0f172a, also the `theme-color`/tile colour) page, `text-slate-400` body, `text-slate-200` headings/emphasis, `text-slate-500` micro-labels, `text-slate-700` for the deliberately-low-contrast 'time travel' teaser, teal-300/teal-400 as the single accent (also the selection colour: `selection:bg-teal-300 selection:text-teal-900`), and `bg-yellow-500` reserved solely for the skip link so it is unmissable on focus. Typography is a single family: Inter, self-hosted through `next/font` (9 preloaded .woff2 subsets, a size-adjusted fallback, zero external font requests), with a `ui-monospace` stack only for micro-labels. Type is set tight — `tracking-tight` on the h1/h2, `uppercase tracking-widest` on the nav and eyebrows. The colophon names Inter explicitly and links to rsms.me/inter.
motion: Deliberately small and correct. Motion is limited to CSS transitions on links/buttons, a `fadeIn` keyframe with a staircase of `delay-[50ms]`…`delay-[300ms]` utilities for staggered entrance, hover/focus translations on arrow icons, the cursor-following spotlight gradient (`transition duration-300`), the list-dimming opacity change, and a spinning Tardis GIF plus a portal effect inside the 'time travel' dialog (the portal is credited in the markup to CodePen pen 'A Portal to Tomorrow' by @jasesmith). No scroll-jacking, no parallax, no autoplaying video, no animation library — the only 'motion' dependency is Tailwind's own transition utilities. `prefers-reduced-motion` IS respected, and in the correct direction: Tailwind's preflight scopes the global transition block inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`, the `fadeIn` keyframes are likewise gated to `no-preference`, and the author additionally hand-applies `motion-reduce:transition-none` to the animated arrow icons and underline transitions. A reduced-motion visitor gets a fully static, fully functional page.
responsiveness_mobile: Fully responsive and the format degrades gracefully because the format is a document. The desktop two-pane split (`lg:flex lg:justify-between`, sticky 48% rail + scrolling 52% column) collapses to a single stacked column below `lg`; padding steps down through `px-6 md:px-12` and `py-12 md:py-16 lg:py-0`; project cards go from an 8-column grid with a thumbnail to a stacked layout (`sm:grid-cols-8` → 1 column, with `sm:order-2` reordering so text precedes image); the tech-tag rows wrap. Three desktop-only affordances are cleanly dropped rather than broken: the cursor spotlight (`lg:absolute`, effectively off on touch), the list hover-dim (`lg:group-hover/list:opacity-50`), and the Korok custom cursor (`lg:cursor-[url(...)]`). Two real mobile costs: (1) the in-page nav is `hidden lg:block`, so a phone visitor has no jump links and no menu button — they must scroll the whole document, and there is no back-to-top; the mitigation is that the sticky section headings become visible on small screens (`lg:sr-only` inverts). (2) The /archive page is a wide 5-column table, which is the one layout on the site that is uncomfortable on a narrow viewport [uncertain]. Payload is tiny on any connection, so mobile performance is a non-issue.
framework_hosting: Next.js (Pages Router) with Tailwind CSS, built as a fully static export — the served `__NEXT_DATA__` carries `"nextExport": true, "autoExport": true`, and there is no server-rendered data, no API route and no `getServerSideProps`. Exact Next major is not exposed; the `next-head-count` meta and the `pages/_app` + `pages/index` chunk naming place it on the Pages Router, so Next 12/13-era rather than App Router [uncertain]. Fonts via `next/font` (self-hosted Inter, size-adjust fallback); images via `next/image` served from the built-in `/_next/image` optimizer at `w=640&q=75`; icons are an inline SVG sprite (`<use>`); a dialog component supplies the 'time travel' modal (`DialogOverlay` + `portal-inner`, i.e. a Reach-UI-style dialog) [uncertain]. Hosting: Vercel (`server: Vercel`, `x-vercel-cache: HIT`, edge `fra1`), with HSTS `max-age=63072000`. Custom domain is the owner's own full name on a `.com` — the strongest possible personal-brand TLD signal — and she additionally keeps every prior generation live on subdomains (v1/v2/v3/v4.brittanychiang.com), which is itself a hosting decision worth noting. `sitemap.xml` is served; `robots.txt` returns 404. The colophon states the stack in plain English on the page: 'Loosely designed in Figma and coded in Visual Studio Code by yours truly. Built with Next.js and Tailwind CSS, deployed with Vercel. All text is set in the Inter typeface.'
performance_a11y: Performance: near-exemplary and the direct opposite of the heavy-portfolio genre. The document is 64.2 KB raw / ~11 KB over the wire; CSS 29 KB raw / 6.4 KB compressed; the whole JS payload for the homepage is ~554 KB raw but ~146 KB compressed across 8 chunks (framework 46.6 KB, main 29.1 KB, _app 34.6 KB, page 12.7 KB, shared 13.2 KB + small), plus a legacy polyfills chunk served `nomodule`. Nine images total, all routed through next/image at 640 px, plus one small GIF. Zero third-party requests except a single async GA4 call — no external fonts, no CDN scripts, no embeds. Fully static, served from Vercel's edge cache. Accessibility: this is the site's actual thesis and it holds up under inspection. A real skip link is the first focusable element (`href="#content"`, `-translate-x-full` → `focus-visible:translate-x-0`, high-contrast yellow) and `<main id="content">` receives it. Heading order is clean and singular (one `<h1>`, then `<h2>` per section, `<h3>` per item) with the desktop-redundant section headings preserved via `lg:sr-only` rather than deleted. 100% alt-text coverage — 9 images, 9 `alt` attributes, all descriptive ('Halcyon Theme homepage hero with screenshot of VS Code editor', 'Spinning Tardis from Doctor Who'), and purely decorative SVGs carry `aria-hidden="true"` (40 instances). Landmark and grouping labels are everywhere: `aria-label` on 'In-page jump links', 'Work experience', 'Selected projects', 'Blog posts', 'Social media', 'Related links', 'Technologies used'. Every external link is annotated '(opens in a new tab)' inside its accessible name and carries `rel="noreferrer noopener"`. Focus management is explicit — the codebase uses `focus-visible:` variants (not just `:hover`) on the nav rule, arrow translations and link colours, so keyboard traversal produces the same affordances as the mouse. `prefers-reduced-motion` is honoured. `lang="en"` set. The residual weaknesses are minor: body text is slate-400 on slate-900 (passes AA for normal text but is not AAA), the 'Looking for a different site? Go back in time...' teaser is intentionally slate-700 on slate-900 and fails contrast, and the /archive table is dense.
analytics_instrumentation: Google Analytics 4 only — an inline `gtag` bootstrap in `<head>` configuring measurement ID `G-4FFCWEC2WB` with `page_path`, present on every route including the 404. No Plausible, no Umami, no Fathom, no Vercel Analytics or Speed Insights, no session replay, no cookie/consent banner. One Google Search Console verification meta tag (`google-site-verification`). The only other outbound runtime call is a client-side `fetch` to `api.github.com` for live star counts (see project_presentation).
project_presentation:
A two-tier system — 4 curated cards on the homepage, ~25 rows in a full archive — and the tiering is the sharpest content decision on the site.

TIER 1 — homepage 'Projects', 4 entries, each an 8-column grid: a 640 px `next/image` thumbnail in a bordered rounded frame, a title that is itself the primary link, 2–3 sentences of plain-language description, a row of tech pills, and where applicable an extra 'related link' with a proof badge. The four: (1) 'Build a Spotify Connected App' — her paid Newline video course, described by curriculum ('REST APIs, user auth flows, Node, Express, React, Styled Components'); (2) 'Spotify Profile' — the React/Express/Spotify-API/Heroku web app; (3) 'Halcyon Theme' — the editor theme, carrying an inline proof badge '100k+ Installs' whose accessible name is 'Over 100,000 installs on Visual Studio Code Marketplace (opens in a new tab)', linking to the actual Marketplace listing; (4) 'brittanychiang.com (v4)' — her own previous site, described as 'An old portfolio site built with Gatsby with 6k+ stars and 3k+ forks', tagged Gatsby / Styled Components / Netlify, linking to v4.brittanychiang.com. Note the self-referential move: the portfolio's fourth project is the portfolio's own previous version.

LIVE STAR COUNT: for GitHub-backed cards a small client component fetches `https://api.github.com/repos/bchiang7/{repo}` on mount, reads `stargazers_count`, and renders it beside a star icon with the accessible label '{n} stars on GitHub (opens in a new tab)'. This is a self-updating social-proof number rather than a hardcoded brag — the standout instrumentation idea on the site. (Its cost is visible: the hardcoded prose still says '6k+ stars and 3k+ forks' while the repo is now at ~8.3k stars / ~4.2k forks, so the static copy has drifted below the live number.)

TIER 2 — /archive ('All Projects'), a 5-column table: Year / Project / Made at / Built with / Link, ~25 rows spanning 2015–2023, each naming the employer (mostly Upstatement) and the exact stack, with the deliverable's production URL as the link. Examples: Emerson Collective (2023, Next.js/TS/SCSS/Contentful, emersoncollective.com), Harvard Business School Next.js site (2023, hbs.edu), HBS Design System (2022, Storybook/React/TS — no link, correctly, because it is internal), Threadable (2022, React Native/Rails/Firebase, App Store link), Pratt (2022, WordPress Multisite/Timber/Gutenberg, pratt.edu), Everytown Gun Law Rankings (2022, WordPress/Timber/PHP/Airtable API), Koala Health (2021, Next.js/TS/Redux Toolkit/Stripe/Algolia/Firebase Auth/Formik/Vercel).

LIVE-DEMO AVAILABILITY: high but honest rather than total. Client work links to the real production site (the strongest possible demo, hosted by the client). Personal projects link to their live host — Netlify (halcyon-theme.netlify.app), Heroku (spotify-profile.herokuapp.com — a legacy host, and the one link most likely to be dead or degraded [uncertain]), the VS Code Marketplace, the App Store, Google Play, and newline.co for the course. Internal/design-system work has NO link, and that omission is the correct signal rather than a gap.

What is absent by design: no per-project case-study pages, no problem/solution/outcome narrative, no screenshots beyond a single thumbnail, no GitHub repo link on most cards. The credibility carrier is the named client plus the live production URL, not prose.
resume_integration_mode: Both — and this is a notable strength relative to the genre. The Experience section is a complete inline HTML résumé: 6 dated roles (2015 → present), each with employer link, role title (including internal progressions rendered as sub-titles, e.g. Upstatement's Lead Engineer / Senior Engineer / Engineer), an achievement paragraph, and per-role tech tags — all real, selectable, crawlable text. Alongside it, 'View Full Résumé' links to `/resume.pdf`, a 2-page, 1.19 MB PDF exported from Figma (Producer: 3-Heights PDF Optimization Shell; `/Font` present, zero raster images, `/ToUnicode` maps present). ATS-parseability: probable but not certain — the fonts are subset-embedded from a Figma export, which is the classic source of garbled ATS extraction, though the presence of ToUnicode CMaps suggests a compliant parser will get clean text [uncertain]. The 1.19 MB weight for a 2-page text-only document is itself a small tell of the Figma pipeline. Practically the site hedges well: even if the PDF parses badly, the HTML Experience section is fully machine-readable.
proof_verifiability: Strong, and achieved almost entirely by outbound linking rather than assertion. Concrete mechanisms: (1) every employer is a live hyperlink (klaviyo.com, upstatement.com, apple.com/apple-music, starry.com, us.mullenlowe.com, scout.camd.northeastern.edu); (2) the Apple co-op claim about the Apple Music embeddable web player is backed by three third-party citations placed inline in the role description — the MusicKit.js developer docs, a 9to5Mac article dated 2018-06-03, and a Verge article dated 2017-10-05 — i.e. press coverage of the shipped feature, which is an unusually rigorous way to substantiate an internship; (3) the Starry role links to Google Play for the app and to Starry's own product blog post about the ScreenTime 2.0 feature she names; (4) the Klaviyo role links to the specific product she says she helped build (klaviyo.com/composer); (5) the Halcyon 100k-installs claim links to the Marketplace page that displays the count; (6) the v4 stars/forks claim is verifiable, and moreover the live GitHub API fetch renders the current number on the page; (7) /archive names the client for every project and links the shipped site, so any claim can be checked against a real artifact; (8) the four Writing entries link to the published articles on Medium and klaviyo.tech. Residual gaps: the archive's 'Made at' attribution does not distinguish her individual contribution from the studio team's, and the Experience prose uses collective verbs ('Build, style, and ship…') without per-project ownership — normal for agency work, but it means the granularity of personal credit is unverifiable from the site alone. No testimonials, no references, no awards claimed.
quantified_impact: Sparse and deliberately so — three numbers in total, each verifiable and none inflated. (1) '100k+ Installs' on the Halcyon theme, linked to the VS Code Marketplace listing. (2) '6k+ stars and 3k+ forks' for the v4 portfolio repo, plus a live-fetched star count from the GitHub API rendered in the card; the hardcoded figure is now conservative (the repo sits near 8.3k stars / 4.2k forks). (3) Dates and durations throughout the Experience section, which quantify tenure and progression (6 years at Upstatement across three titles). What is entirely absent: no user counts, no revenue, no latency/accuracy/conversion/cost-saved figures, no 'improved X by Y%' anywhere. The Experience bullets describe scope and responsibility ('components used to construct Klaviyo's frontend, across the whole product', 'leadership within engineering department') rather than outcomes. For a frontend/design-system engineer at a product company this is a defensible trade — the metrics that matter (adoption of a component library, a11y compliance) are internal and unpublishable — but it does mean the site would score poorly on a naive 'quantified impact' rubric, and it is the clearest thing a hackathon-style portfolio should NOT copy from her.
content_freshness: Fresh and maintained. The homepage HTML carries `Last-Modified: 2026-07-17` (about two weeks before this research), served from Vercel edge cache. The Writing section's newest entry is dated 2026 ('Welcome to the AI Parade', on Medium) — a same-year publication, which is the clearest recency proof on the page. The About section carries an explicit present-tense status ('Currently, I'm a Senior Frontend Engineer at Klaviyo, where I work on our design system and help build new products, like Composer') and the Experience section's top row reads '2024 — Present'. There is no dedicated /now page, no 'currently working on' widget, and no last-updated stamp in the footer. One structural freshness feature: the live GitHub star fetch means at least one number on the page can never go stale. One small staleness tell: /archive's newest row is 2023, so nothing from the Klaviyo era has been added to the project archive; and the v4 star/fork prose has drifted.
writing_tone: Warm, plain, first-person, low-ego, and specific — professional without corporate register. Opens 'Hi there! I'm Brittany, and I like building things.' Claims are phrased as craft rather than status: 'expertise in crafting accessible, pixel-perfect user interfaces', 'a sharp eye for the little details that separate a good product from an exceptional one', 'I enjoy working most at the intersection of design and engineering'. Employers are described generically before being named ('from product studios to startups and large tech companies'; the accessible names of those links read 'digital product studio', 'start-up', 'huge corporation' — a small, dry joke). Personality is confined to exactly one paragraph and delivered with restraint: 'In my spare time, you can usually find me climbing, playing tennis, hanging out with my wife and two cats, or running around Hyrule searching for Korok seeds' — where 'Korok seeds' is an interactive easter egg (see standout_features). Zero buzzwords, no 'passionate about', no 'ninja/rockstar', no exclamation-heavy hype, no AI-generated cadence. Résumé bullets use present-tense active verbs and name real clients. The colophon is modest and generous, crediting tools by name and linking each.
standout_features:
Ranked by borrowability for a conventional SE portfolio.

ESSENTIALLY FREE AND WORTH COPYING IMMEDIATELY:
1. Skip link as the first focusable element, styled to be unmissable — `href="#content"`, `-translate-x-full` off-canvas until `focus-visible:translate-x-0`, high-contrast `bg-yellow-500`. Six lines of markup and the single loudest a11y signal a frontend candidate can send.
2. '(opens in a new tab)' baked into every external link's `aria-label`, with `rel="noreferrer noopener"`. Mechanical, invisible to sighted users, and it demonstrates the exact discipline the résumé claims.
3. Tech tags attached to jobs and projects instead of a standalone Skills section. Every technology is anchored to where it was actually used, which quietly kills the credibility problem of the flat skills cloud.
4. Third-party press/docs citations inline in a role description — the Apple co-op line links MusicKit.js docs + 9to5Mac + The Verge. Turns an internship bullet into a cited fact. Costs three `<a>` tags.
5. `focus-visible:` variants applied everywhere `hover:` is, so keyboard users get identical affordances (nav rule extension, arrow translation, colour change). Most portfolios style hover only.
6. `lg:sr-only` on section headings: the heading is visually redundant on desktop (the sticky rail names the section) but is retained for screen readers and becomes visible on mobile where the rail is gone. A neat both-ways solution instead of deleting or duplicating.
7. A plain-English colophon naming and linking the stack (Figma, VS Code, Next.js, Tailwind, Vercel, Inter). Cheapest authenticity signal available.
8. Two-tier project structure: 4 curated cards on the homepage + a complete /archive table (Year / Project / Made at / Built with / Link). Solves 'do I show the small stuff?' without diluting the headline set — and the table is the most recruiter-legible artifact on the whole site.
9. Correct `prefers-reduced-motion` handling: rely on Tailwind's `no-preference`-gated preflight and add explicit `motion-reduce:transition-none` on the few hand-animated elements.

CHEAP, HIGH-CHARM, MODERATE EFFORT:
10. Live GitHub star count fetched client-side from `api.github.com/repos/...` and rendered with an accessible label. Self-updating social proof; no build step, no token.
11. The 'time travel' easter egg: a low-contrast teaser ('Looking for a different site? Go back in time...') opens a dialog listing v1–v4 of the site, each kept live on its own subdomain, decorated with a spinning Tardis GIF and a portal effect honestly credited in the markup to a CodePen pen by @jasesmith. It converts eight years of iteration into a browsable narrative of growth — arguably the single most charming idea here, and it doubles as evidence of longevity.
12. The Korok seed easter egg: hovering the phrase 'Korok seeds' in the About paragraph swaps the cursor to a Korok PNG (`lg:cursor-[url('/images/koroks/Elma.png'),_pointer]`) and randomises each letter's colour across eleven Tailwind hues on hover. Pure delight, ~15 lines, desktop-only and therefore free on mobile.
13. Group-hover list dimming — hovering one Experience/Project row drops the sibling rows to `opacity-50` and lifts a soft card behind the hovered one. Creates focus without any JS or layout shift.
14. Cursor-following radial-gradient spotlight, `lg:` only. One fixed div and a mousemove handler.
15. Keeping every previous version of the site live at v1/v2/v3/v4 subdomains, and listing the previous one as a project with its own star count.

THE STRUCTURAL LESSON: this site's power is that the medium proves the claim with almost no budget. She claims 'accessible, pixel-perfect' and the site is measurably accessible (skip link, 9/9 alt text, labelled landmarks, focus-visible parity, reduced-motion support) and measurably light (~11 KB HTML, ~146 KB compressed JS, one third-party request). That is why it is the most-cloned SE portfolio in existence — the layout is copyable in an afternoon, and unlike the 3D/game genre nothing in it trades legibility for spectacle. The trap for imitators is that they copy the visual layer (dark slate, teal pills, sticky rail, hover dimming) and skip the two things that actually make it work: the a11y implementation underneath, and the outbound citations that make every claim checkable.
originality_vs_template: Fully custom and the origin of a lineage rather than a member of one. Brittany Chiang has shipped five generations of her own site (v1 HTML, v2 Jekyll, v3 Jekyll/SCSS, v4 Gatsby + Styled Components, current v5 Next.js + Tailwind), each a from-scratch rebuild in a different stack — the iteration history is itself part of the content. The v4 build (github.com/bchiang7/v4, ~8.3k stars / ~4.2k forks) became the single most-forked personal-portfolio repo in the ecosystem and spawned a large derivative population: repos and articles explicitly framed as 'inspired by Brittany Chiang', ports to Vue and other frameworks, and portfolio-inspiration galleries that list her as a canonical entry. The current v5 layout — dark slate, sticky left rail, teal accents, hover-dimmed lists — is now widely imitated in turn. If a portfolio in the research set resembles this one, the causality runs from here outward.
source_available: Partially, and the distinction matters. The CURRENT site (v5) has no public repository — `bchiang7`'s public repos include v1, v2, v3 (`bchiang7/v3`), `bchiang7.github.io` and `v4`, but no v5/current-site repo, and the live build's `_next` chunk hashes have no public counterpart. So the site being examined is closed-source. Every PREVIOUS generation is open: `bchiang7/v4` (Gatsby, ~8.3k stars / ~4.2k forks, MIT, still actively receiving issues in 2026), `bchiang7/bchiang7.github.io` (Jekyll, ~850 stars), `bchiang7/v3`, `bchiang7/v2`, `bchiang7/v1`. Adjacent dogfooding is strong regardless: `spotify-profile` (~720 stars), `octoprofile` (~500), `halcyon-vscode` (~240) and `halcyon-site` are all public, so the projects the site advertises are independently inspectable even though the site itself is not. Reading the closure charitably: she open-sourced v4, watched it become a template farm with 49 open issues from forkers, and chose not to repeat that with v5 [uncertain].
contact_methods: Notably minimal — there is no contact section at all. No contact form, no email address anywhere in the served HTML or JS (a grep for `mailto:` and for any `@`-address returns nothing), no phone, no calendar link, no 'get in touch' CTA, and no availability statement. The only reachability surface is a horizontal social icon row anchored at the bottom of the sticky left rail (i.e. persistently visible on desktop, and at the end of the scroll on mobile): GitHub (github.com/bchiang7), LinkedIn (linkedin.com/in/bchiang7), CodePen (codepen.io/bchiang7), Instagram (instagram.com/bchiang7) and Goodreads (a personal reading profile — an unusual, humanising inclusion). Each icon has an `aria-label` and `rel="noreferrer noopener"`. An X/Twitter icon exists in the SVG sprite and the meta tags still declare `twitter:creator`/`twitter:site` as `@bchiang7`, but no X link is rendered in the social row — a removed channel whose scaffolding remains. pii_exposure: Minimal to none — among the cleanest in the set. No email address, no phone number, no postal address, no employer-internal information, and no photograph of the owner appears anywhere on the site. Real name is intentionally public (it is the brand and the domain). The résumé PDF at /resume.pdf is publicly downloadable and would conventionally carry contact details, but the on-site surface itself exposes nothing scrapeable [uncertain — the PDF's own contact block was not extractable from the Figma-exported font encoding]. Voluntarily disclosed personal detail is limited to two sentences in the About paragraph (climbing, tennis, 'my wife and two cats', Zelda) plus a linked Goodreads profile that reveals reading history — mild, chosen, and reversible. Visitor-side privacy: Google Analytics 4 runs with no cookie or consent banner, and the client-side GitHub API fetch discloses each visitor's IP to GitHub; there is no other third-party call.
